title: No Map for This
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 29 of 40
content:
The map was upside down.

Greg denied this until the coastline began moving in the wrong direction, at which point he announced that he had discovered an exciting alternate route.

"An alternate route to where?" I asked.

"Adventure."

"That sounds suspiciously like getting lost."

"It's only getting lost if you don't enjoy it."

The van rattled along a highway outside Beach City, its radio fading between songs. We'd left for a short weekend trip, planning to see a small music festival and return before Monday. I had packed food, medication, a charger and an actual paper itinerary. Greg had packed three guitar picks, two shirts and a bag of chips that he had already eaten.

At the first gas station, we discovered the festival had moved its opening set an hour earlier. Greg checked the flyer twice.

"That's odd. They told me they'd hold a place."

I looked at him. "You're performing?"

"Maybe. I got invited. I was going to tell you."

"Greg."

He grimaced. "I know. I thought if I said it out loud, the trip would become about me being the old Mr. Universe again."

I shut the glove compartment. I was annoyed, and also worried. The plan we'd made together was supposed to be a little breathing space. I didn't want to find out halfway there that he expected me to be part of a show.

"I'm glad somebody invited you," I said. "I want you to be able to play. But I'm not a surprise backup singer."

"Right. No surprise backup singers."

"And I need to know the schedule before deciding whether I want to go."

He found a pencil. We wrote down the actual travel time, the festival's published hours and the nearest inexpensive place to sleep. I called the organizer from the station phone while Greg waited beside me.

They had space for him in an afternoon set, without any obligation to perform the old hits. If he wanted to play, he could confirm by noon. If not, the invitation would remain a friendly one.

"That's a real choice," I told him.

He looked at the flyer. "Yeah. It is."

We stopped at a roadside diner because neither of us was in a state to make decisions on an empty stomach. The waitress gave us coffee that tasted like she was mad at somebody. Greg drank it cheerfully. I added enough sugar to qualify as structural repair.

"Are you disappointed?" he asked.

"A little. I wanted a weekend that wasn't another performance."

"Me too."

"You can love music and not want to be somebody's nostalgia act."

He stirred his coffee. "I think part of me wanted them to remember me. Then I got scared they'd remember somebody I can't be anymore."

I reached across the table, palm up. He took my hand.

"I'm here for the person who got the map upside down," I said. "I don't need the old poster."

"Good, because the poster had terrible hair."

"You have terrible hair now."

"True. Consistency."

We called the organizer again and accepted the afternoon slot. Greg would play two new songs and one older one he actually wanted to perform. I would be in the audience if I chose. Nobody would list me as his duet partner without asking.

The organizer met us at the festival gate with a clipboard and an apology. The earlier schedule had been published before he checked with every performer; two musicians had already declined the new times.

"Can you still play the afternoon slot?" he asked Greg.

"Yes. Two new songs, one old one. That's what we agreed."

The organizer nodded and corrected the sheet. He asked whether I wanted to help with the sound desk. I said I wanted to watch from the audience instead. The question didn't make him angry, and I was glad of it.

We had an hour before the set, so Greg and I walked to the little park beside the basketball court. A few teenagers were practicing chords on the steps. One recognized him from an old poster and asked whether he still played the same songs.

"Some of them," he said. "You got any favorites?"

The kid began a tune from a different band entirely. Greg laughed and offered one piece of advice about keeping the rhythm steady, then moved on rather than turning their afternoon into his performance.

"You're good with them," I said.

"I'm good with people who care about music more than whether somebody's famous."

I considered that. We'd traveled to a new town with a real budget, a return date and other commitments waiting for us. I didn't need this weekend to prove our relationship was extraordinary.

"Could we go to that bookstore after you play?" I asked.

"Absolutely. If it's still open."

"And if the concert runs late?"

"Then we'll decide together. No surprise extra set."

I smiled. We were both getting better at keeping promises small enough to be real. He took my hand as we walked back, the sound of somebody tuning a guitar drifting across the court.

"Thanks for coming," he said.

"I wanted to."

He looked almost startled by that simple answer, then squeezed my hand once.

The rest of the drive was quieter. We passed a field of tall grass and a little town where somebody had painted a mural across the side of a diner. Greg told me about a tour that had gone wrong years before, then let the story stay wrong without polishing it into a triumph.

At the motel, the air conditioner rattled every time it started. I checked the room's door and the route back to the parking lot. The bed was narrow, but the sheets were clean. We put the map on the dresser with the route facing the right direction.

"You know," Greg said, "we could still turn around tomorrow."

"We could."

"Would you want to?"

"I want to see the show. I also want to know we can leave if it stops being fun."

"Deal."

Our relationship had room for other people and obligations. We had talked openly about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory. The important part wasn't pretending we would always choose the same trip; it was asking rather than assuming.

At the park, the sound technician discovered that one of the outlets had no ground. She taped it off and asked the organizer to use the inspected circuit on the opposite wall.

Greg saw the cable crossing the walkway and shook his head. “Hey, we can't leave that there. Someone's going to take a dive before I even get to the bad jokes.”

He helped reroute the lead behind the portable stage. It took ten minutes, and the organizer began looking at the clock.

“We're already late,” she said.

“Yeah,” Greg replied. “A late show beats an ambulance. Trust me, nobody's coming for the stunt work.”

I had expected him to be resentful after the surprise booking conversation. Instead he asked whether the teenager from the park could borrow a chair for the opening song, and he waited while the stage manager checked where it would fit.

“You didn't need me to run sound,” I told him.

“Didn't want you to. You said you wanted to listen.” He shrugged. “I know, I know. A musician respecting an audience member's choices. They're gonna kick me out of the union.”

I tugged him gently by the hem of his shirt. He turned, smiling, and for a second the noise of the crowd fell away. His hair was wind-tangled; he had a streak of grease on one wrist from helping with the cable stand.

“You're very attractive when you don't volunteer my entire afternoon,” I said.

He blinked, then almost dropped his pick. “Whoa. Remind me to put that on a poster.”

“Do not.”

He kissed the back of my hand, clumsy with the guitar balanced against his hip, and hurried toward the stage before the organizer had to call his name again.


The festival was small, with a stage beside an old basketball court and a volunteer checking the safety of the power cables. Greg played without introducing me as a prize or an answer to his past. He made an earnest joke about his hair. The audience groaned and applauded anyway.

I sat on a folding chair near the side, cheering so loudly that he missed the first beat of the second song.

Afterward he kissed me when I stepped close enough and asked.

We spent the evening walking through the town instead of staying for every act. There were cheap postcards and a bookstore with an enormous cat sleeping in the window. Greg bought me a postcard showing a road disappearing over a hill.

"To remember the great adventure," he said.

"To remember the map was upside down."

"That too."

In the morning, he drew a crooked star near the diner on our map. Then he folded it properly and handed it to me.

We got home with money left for groceries, a song he'd enjoyed playing and enough stories to laugh about without pretending any of them had changed our whole lives.
